Bela Education

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A bill that sparked big debate with some saying it will cause the end of the government of national unity... but the emotions aside, does Government have the money to implement the controversial Bela

Unique Selling Point:
What's all the hype about the Bela bill if government doesn't even have the money to implement it?

Summary:
Its gonna cost resources... and lot of it... does government have the financial and administrative capacity to implement the controversial Bela Bill? Grade R is now compulsory. In the most ironic turn of events, government earmarks R16 billion necessary to establish infrastructure and appoint teachers to fill the gap. But at the same time, teacher retrenchments are underway. The Western Cape just announced the retrenchment of 2400 teacher due to budget cuts.

Further information:
Two clauses of the Act were set aside for further discussion when president Cyril Ramaphosa signed the Basic Education Laws Amendment (Bela) Bill on Friday the 13th of September. One being admission and the other being the state's power to determine language proposed by a school SGB. The bill is only an amendment of an existing bill and much of it was already included in original bill of 1996. Now, there will be harsher punishment if the bill is not implemented. A parent for example, can now be jailed if a child is not sent to school. The onus was always on the parents, the consequences for failure to adhere, are just made much harsher and many organisations agree on this front. What most organisations, civil groups and activists don't agree with, is certain aspects of the bill that government does not have money to implement. The most concerning is that Grade R is now compulsory and it will cost government nearly 16 million Rand to to enforce this decision. It will mean classrooms and teachers- resources- in the midst of thousands of teachers that have to be laid off over the next few months. In Cape Town alone, over 2500 teachers have been retrenched. So how will funds be reprioritise in a province such as Gauteng, to make room for thousands of Grade R's?

Further to this: If a parent fails to send their children to school, those parents must be identified and the local department of education must visit the parent, trying to establish reasons why the children are not in school. Then the legal system must kick in and parents must be prosecuted, what financial burden will this have on the state?

Homeschooling: If a child is to be homeschooled, the Departmnet must register the home school. Then an assessor must be appointed to asses the homeschool. These are usually senior educators, are they going to be appointed? How many new appointments will this be within the department and how is the state to afford this?

Lastly, if clause 4 and 5 are signed into law in 3 months, what will the financial burden be on schools and how will the state assist the schools financially? For example: if an Afrikaans medium school is forced to admit English or Zulu learners, capacity should be created within the school to accommodate these learners. Who will fund this and if its funded by the state, with what money? or will schools be forced to pay for these shortcomings themselves? will this be a further burden on parents to pay higher school fees?



Extra Budget Items:
This shoot is scattered across days. We speak to the minister of basic education on 27 September. Then we speak to the MEC of education in Gauteng on 30 September and regarding language and admissions, we are able to speak to Afriforum-pivotal in the postponement of the signing of 4 and 5, on 26 September.

Press Release:


On Tuesday, thousands of protesters gathered at the Settlers Monument in Pretoria to protest the controversial Basic Education Laws Amendment Bill. This after President Cyril Ramaphosa signed the Bill into law in September, but recommended that two crucial sections of the Bill, be reviewed. Now two months into the three-month consultation period around sections of the Bela Act, opinions continue to be divided as the future of basic education seemingly hangs in the balance. As time runs out for concerned parties to find a middle ground, will Ramaphosa sign the remaining controversial sections into law?

Script:


UPSOUND: GREENSIDE HIGH CHOIR SINGING NKOSI SIKILELA
UPSOUND: CYRIL RAMAPHOSA: Whatever our disagreements, we all seek a better and more efficient and more equitable education system that best serves the children of South Africa.
UPSOUND: PANYAZA LESUFI: I’m asking you president, politely and respectfully so, sign that law.
UPSOUND: KALLIE KRIEL (AFRIFORUM): The Afrikaans speaking community, we see it as an issue of survival.
UPSOUND: NOMUSA CEMBI (SADTU): Organisations that are lobbying for Afrikaans are being populist when they look at this progressive act, which is to ensure equity.
UPSOUND: EMIHLE MAJIKIJI (SECTION 27): There are so many incredible developments that we could find in BELA if our eyes were not so focused on the wrong things.
UPSOUND: MINISTER SIVIWE GWARUBE: It risks dividing the sector if we don’t resolve the issues around clauses 4 and 5.
UPSOUND: Weg met BELA! Weg met BELA!
VO1: This week, thousands of people marched from the Voortrekker Monument to protest the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act, known as BELA.
UPSOUND: BELA is boos! BELA is boos!
VOX POP: Hulle probeer om Afrikaans uit die land uit te druk en ons Afrikaners gaan dit nie toelaat nie.
VOX POP: We cannot take away the rights of parents, we cannot allow the government to be in charge of everything.
VO2: It’s become a battle over language, identity, and access to education. On one side is a fear that the Act will signal the death of Afrikaans government schools. On the other are those who say those schools fail to meet the needs of their communities.
VOX POP: JOHN STEENHUISEN: Clauses 4 and 5 give too much power to provincial officials and take too much away from communities and parents.
VO3: Signed into law by President Ramaphosa in September, BELA is seen by some as the biggest threat to the Government of National Unity.
VOX POP: GLYNNIS BREYTENBACH: Everybody has to have a red line that you can’t pass. If we reach that line they will do what they have to do.
VO4: It aims to overhaul our education system, from homeschooling to religion in schools, and makes Grade R attendance compulsory. Most of the amendments are uncontroversial.
UPSOUND: MINISTER SIVIWE GWARUBE: Part of the reason why the BELA Act came about is because the education department kept on being taken to court about some of these things, because there wasn’t clarity in the system.
VO5: But two disputed clauses are jeopardising an already fragile power sharing deal... The DA has threatened to withdraw from the GNU if they’re passed in their current form. The standoff has put the new Minister of Basic Education, Siviwe Gwarube, in a difficult position: she’s a member of the DA but, as part of Cabinet, she’s compelled to ensure BELA is implemented.
UPSOUND: MINISTER SIVIWE GWARUBE: So now we have a consolidated piece of legislation so it’s a move in the right direction. But greater consultation needs to be done.
VO6: The contested clauses are Section 4, which gives the Department of Basic Education control over school enrolment, and Section 5, which compels schools to submit their language policies to the department for approval. Both were put on hold for three months to allow for more consultation.
UPSOUND: CYRIL RAMAPHOSA: If a solution is not found, the law stands as I will have signed it today.
UPSOUND: CHARLES MYBURGH (SGB LAERSKOOL LOUIS LEIPOLDT): It would just be an input that you give, the final decisions will be taken elsewhere, especially where you’re trying to protect your culture and your language.
VO7: The Act centralises significant power under the Minister of Basic Education. Critics say this undermines the authority of school governing bodies, or SGBs, which are made up of parents and community members wanting to play an active role in school management. Charles Myburgh is vice chairman of the SGB at a leading Afrikaans primary school in Pretoria.
UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: What are the concerns by those who are opposed to the BELA Act?
CHARLES MYBURGH (SGB LAERSKOOL LOUIS LEIPOLDT): You currently have a grouping of parents that are willing to contribute because they see the benefits. When it’s all been centralised into government, you may not have this voluntary step forward from parents to actually get involved and assist the school, assist the school principal.
VO8: The success of many government schools is driven by proactive SGBs, so if Myburgh is right, there’s reason to be concerned. But its supporters argue that these fears are an over-reaction.
UPSOUND: EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): Part of the controversy surrounding the BELA Bill, if you were to sum it up in one sentence, it's that interesting combination of misinformation and disinformation.
VO9: Emihle Majikija is a legal researcher at public interest organisation, Section 27.
UPSOUND: EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): If you turn to the South African Schools Act, there are already provisions that make it so that provincial departments of education can intervene. In fact, the Constitutional Court has even emphasized that the power of school governing bodies is not subject to, you know, absolute autonomy. What the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act actually does then, in this regard, is that it concretized the principles that the courts have already pronounced on and that are already acceptable in our law.
UPSOUND: SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA (DEPUTY PRINCIPAL, GREENSIDE HIGH SCHOOL): I don’t have any concerns with regards to the BELA Act. We cannot decide on any form of policy, even the school code of conduct, without the validation of our district directors.
VO10: Sibusiso Masombuka is deputy principal of a leading English school in Johannesburg.
UPSOUND: SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA (DEPUTY PRINCIPAL, GREENSIDE HIGH SCHOOL): We are still able to develop our own policies, we just obviously need to adhere to the constitution and everything else that is mandated by the government.
MASA KEKANA: Isn’t that going to delay some of the decision-making?
SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA: It certainly is going to delay the process, I think the state is running quite a lot of schools but I still think that schools, or anybody that is developing a policy in a school, needs to be inclusive.
UPSOUND: NOMUSA CEMBI (SADTU): We are pro-clauses four and five because we believe that these are the clauses that will ensure that learners access education wherever that they want to in South Africa.
VO11: Nomusa Cembi is spokesperson for the South African Democratic Teachers’ Union.
UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: There are concerns that they won't be able to effectively govern some of government's most excellent schools.
NOMUSA CEMBI: We don't believe that this will take away the powers of the SGBs. It’s just that at the end of the day, the department will have the final say. We believe it is crucial that the department has the final say, because some SGBs have abused their power to exclude learners.
UPSOUND EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): There are children who have to cross rivers to access a school. There are children who, in the face of the climate change that is rocking this nation, will probably not be able to have classrooms in the near future. To insist on the fact that in your school, because you have these resources, only your children can go to those schools, it says something about, I guess, Ubuntu in this country.
UPSOUND PROTEST: Ons is hier om te se: Weg met BELA! Weg met BELA!
VO12: But the real crux of the emotion swirling around BELA is language.
VOX POP: I think it’s important that we look at all the languages in the country and put our energy to preserve that rather than forcing us all to speak English.
VOX POP: HEINDRICH WYNGAARD: Everyone who is here is here because Afrikaans is important to them and they won’t allow politicians to dictate the language of their school.
UPSOUND: PANYAZA LESUFI: If you want only Afrikaans in your own school alone, that’s where we differ. And I’ll tell you why I want to differ with you on that one. I don’t want schools for klein basies alone.
VO13: Part of the reason for the uproar is comments like these from former Gauteng education MEC, now provincial premier, Panyaza Lesufi - one of BELA’s biggest supporters.
UPSOUND: PANYAZA LESUFI: The law is simple, all our children must be in the same classroom and taught by the same teacher. What's wrong with that particular proposal?
UPSOUND: KALLIE KRIEL (AFRIFORUM): We believe that the president is getting pressure from those anti-Afrikaans activists like Panyaza Lesufi who openly states that there is no place for a single medium Afrikaans school in the province. And they are out to destroy Afrikaans schools.
VO14: Kallie Kriel is the CEO of Afrikaner interest group, Afriforum, which is concerned that Afrikaans schools will be forced to enrol students who speak other languages - and then to change their language of tuition…phasing out Afrikaans and other languages altogether.
UPSOUND: KALLIE KRIEL (AFRIFORUM): You have a colonial language, the biggest colonial language in the world and everybody is rallying behind that. Local languages that have been developed on African soil, why should they be portrayed as excluding? While in reality many black children go to Afrikaans schools.
MASA KEKANA: But not the majority of them, let's be honest. The majority of black people, black children, don’t speak Afrikaans.
KALLIE KRIEL: Many of them, especially in rural areas, don’t speak English either. Every year you look at the matric results, those schools that have the worst result, those schools with the biggest drop out numbers are schools where children are taught in their second or third language.
UPSOUND: MINISTER SIVIWE GWARUBE: Mother tongue education is extremely important and this is sometimes also what saddens me about this debate is that it’s often divisive because Afrikaans is one of the most widely spoken languages in this country, not just by white South Africans, across the board, there are many South Africans across the board who speak the language. So, you can’t blame parents who say, I want my child to study and learn in the language of their choice.
VO15: But SADTU says that’s exactly what the act is supposed to do.
UPSOUND: NOMUSA CEMBI (SADTU): The department will have to look at the community, what language is being spoken, before it approves the policy that has been drafted by the school governing body.
MASA KEKANA: Do you really believe that if there's more access in Afrikaans schools, it will solve our shortage of schools? Because the bigger issue here is that government isn't building enough schools.
NOMUSA CEMBI: Yes, government isn't building enough schools. But there is this hysteria. It's as if people are now going to rush to the Afrikaans school.
UPSOUND EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): We can't be complaining about schools that are, you know, in a terrible condition, lambasting the government for that, but at the same time saying that, no, you can't come to our schools. A basic education system where you can arbitrarily decide that because you don't speak my language, you can't come into my school and therefore you can't exercise your basic education is... It doesn't make sense.
VO16: And considering the needs of the surrounding community is something many schools already do successfully.
UPSOUND: SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA (DEPUTY PRINCIPAL, GREENSIDE HIGH SCHOOL): We’ve got two languages apart from English that we teach our learners in and it is also that we brought into consideration the community and the kids and where they come from when we put these languages in force in our school.
MASA KEKANA: And what languages are they?
SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA: It is isiZulu, and they can do that at first additional language as well as Afrikaans at first additional language.
VO17: Lesufi declined our request for an interview. His office told us he’s not interested in answering questions about - in their words - organisations trying to build white enclaves.
VOX POP: We’re saying to every party in the GNU, if BELA is implemented with 4 and 5, you must reconsider your alliance with the GNU. Because we can’t have education that tramples our children.
VO18: The battle to find a middle ground continues with weeks to go before the President’s deadline.
UPSOUND: MINISTER SIVIWE GWARUBE: My argument had been to say, send it back to parliament, let parliament be the one that panel beats this writing. That’s why the wording of clause 4 and 5 need to be refined. Because it needs to make it clear, that it will not be a phasing out of a language but adding languages.
VOX POP: MINISTER GAYTON MACKENZIE: I don’t even know if I f****n like John. But one thing I do know - he f****n likes me more than Malema. That is proof, clear proof, that the GNU can work. We will find each other no matter what.
VO19: Fighting talk from GNU Minister Gayton Mackenzie. And while the effect on state schools remains to be seen, the Act’s supporters are impatient to see it implemented in full.
UPSOUND EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): It is really, really, really important for the transformation of basic education in this country. The National Assembly passed it, the NCOP passed it. There was already public consultation. Democracy worked and gave us the Bela Bill. What more can you possibly ask for?

CHARLES MYBURGH (SGB LAERSKOOL LOUIS LEIPOLDT): You currently have a grouping of parents that are willing to contribute because they see the benefits. When it’s all been centralised into government, you may not have this voluntary step forward from parents to actually get involved and assist the school, assist the school principal. VO8: The success of many government schools is driven by proactive SGBs, so if Myburgh is right, there’s reason to be concerned. But its supporters argue that these fears are an over-reaction. UPSOUND: EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): Part of the controversy surrounding the BELA Bill, if you were to sum it up in one sentence, it's that interesting combination of misinformation and disinformation. VO9: Emihle Majikija is a legal researcher at public interest organisation, Section 27. UPSOUND: EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): If you turn to the South African Schools Act, there are already provisions that make it so that provincial departments of education can intervene. In fact, the Constitutional Court has even emphasized that the power of school governing bodies is not subject to, you know, absolute autonomy. What the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act actually does then, in this regard, is that it concretized the principles that the courts have already pronounced on and that are already acceptable in our law. UPSOUND: SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA (DEPUTY PRINCIPAL, GREENSIDE HIGH SCHOOL): I don’t have any concerns with regards to the BELA Act. We cannot decide on any form of policy, even the school code of conduct, without the validation of our district directors. VO10: Sibusiso Masombuka is deputy principal of a leading English school in Johannesburg. UPSOUND: SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA (DEPUTY PRINCIPAL, GREENSIDE HIGH SCHOOL): We are still able to develop our own policies, we just obviously need to adhere to the constitution and everything else that is mandated by the government. MASA KEKANA: Isn’t that going to delay some of the decision-making? SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA: It certainly is going to delay the process, I think the state is running quite a lot of schools but I still think that schools, or anybody that is developing a policy in a school, needs to be inclusive. UPSOUND: NOMUSA CEMBI (SADTU): We are pro-clauses four and five because we believe that these are the clauses that will ensure that learners access education wherever that they want to in South Africa. VO11: Nomusa Cembi is spokesperson for the South African Democratic Teachers’ Union. UPSOUND: MASA KEKANA: There are concerns that they won't be able to effectively govern some of government's most excellent schools. NOMUSA CEMBI: We don't believe that this will take away the powers of the SGBs. It’s just that at the end of the day, the department will have the final say. We believe it is crucial that the department has the final say, because some SGBs have abused their power to exclude learners. UPSOUND EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): There are children who have to cross rivers to access a school. There are children who, in the face of the climate change that is rocking this nation, will probably not be able to have classrooms in the near future. To insist on the fact that in your school, because you have these resources, only your children can go to those schools, it says something about, I guess, Ubuntu in this country. UPSOUND PROTEST: Ons is hier om te se: Weg met BELA! Weg met BELA! VO12: But the real crux of the emotion swirling around BELA is language. VOX POP: I think it’s important that we look at all the languages in the country and put our energy to preserve that rather than forcing us all to speak English. VOX POP: HEINDRICH WYNGAARD: Everyone who is here is here because Afrikaans is important to them and they won’t allow politicians to dictate the language of their school. UPSOUND: PANYAZA LESUFI: If you want only Afrikaans in your own school alone, that’s where we differ. And I’ll tell you why I want to differ with you on that one. I don’t want schools for klein basies alone. VO13: Part of the reason for the uproar is comments like these from former Gauteng education MEC, now provincial premier, Panyaza Lesufi - one of BELA’s biggest supporters. UPSOUND: PANYAZA LESUFI: The law is simple, all our children must be in the same classroom and taught by the same teacher. What's wrong with that particular proposal? UPSOUND: KALLIE KRIEL (AFRIFORUM): We believe that the president is getting pressure from those anti-Afrikaans activists like Panyaza Lesufi who openly states that there is no place for a single medium Afrikaans school in the province. And they are out to destroy Afrikaans schools. VO14: Kallie Kriel is the CEO of Afrikaner interest group, Afriforum, which is concerned that Afrikaans schools will be forced to enrol students who speak other languages - and then to change their language of tuition…phasing out Afrikaans and other languages altogether. UPSOUND: KALLIE KRIEL (AFRIFORUM): You have a colonial language, the biggest colonial language in the world and everybody is rallying behind that. Local languages that have been developed on African soil, why should they be portrayed as excluding? While in reality many black children go to Afrikaans schools. MASA KEKANA: But not the majority of them, let's be honest. The majority of black people, black children, don’t speak Afrikaans. KALLIE KRIEL: Many of them, especially in rural areas, don’t speak English either. Every year you look at the matric results, those schools that have the worst result, those schools with the biggest drop out numbers are schools where children are taught in their second or third language. UPSOUND: MINISTER SIVIWE GWARUBE: Mother tongue education is extremely important and this is sometimes also what saddens me about this debate is that it’s often divisive because Afrikaans is one of the most widely spoken languages in this country, not just by white South Africans, across the board, there are many South Africans across the board who speak the language. So, you can’t blame parents who say, I want my child to study and learn in the language of their choice. VO15: But SADTU says that’s exactly what the act is supposed to do. UPSOUND: NOMUSA CEMBI (SADTU): The department will have to look at the community, what language is being spoken, before it approves the policy that has been drafted by the school governing body. MASA KEKANA: Do you really believe that if there's more access in Afrikaans schools, it will solve our shortage of schools? Because the bigger issue here is that government isn't building enough schools. NOMUSA CEMBI: Yes, government isn't building enough schools. But there is this hysteria. It's as if people are now going to rush to the Afrikaans school. UPSOUND EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): We can't be complaining about schools that are, you know, in a terrible condition, lambasting the government for that, but at the same time saying that, no, you can't come to our schools. A basic education system where you can arbitrarily decide that because you don't speak my language, you can't come into my school and therefore you can't exercise your basic education is... It doesn't make sense. VO16: And considering the needs of the surrounding community is something many schools already do successfully. UPSOUND: SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA (DEPUTY PRINCIPAL, GREENSIDE HIGH SCHOOL): We’ve got two languages apart from English that we teach our learners in and it is also that we brought into consideration the community and the kids and where they come from when we put these languages in force in our school. MASA KEKANA: And what languages are they? SIBUSISO MASOMBUKA: It is isiZulu, and they can do that at first additional language as well as Afrikaans at first additional language. VO17: Lesufi declined our request for an interview. His office told us he’s not interested in answering questions about - in their words - organisations trying to build white enclaves. VOX POP: We’re saying to every party in the GNU, if BELA is implemented with 4 and 5, you must reconsider your alliance with the GNU. Because we can’t have education that tramples our children. VO18: The battle to find a middle ground continues with weeks to go before the President’s deadline. UPSOUND: MINISTER SIVIWE GWARUBE: My argument had been to say, send it back to parliament, let parliament be the one that panel beats this writing. That’s why the wording of clause 4 and 5 need to be refined. Because it needs to make it clear, that it will not be a phasing out of a language but adding languages. VOX POP: MINISTER GAYTON MACKENZIE: I don’t even know if I f****n like John. But one thing I do know - he f****n likes me more than Malema. That is proof, clear proof, that the GNU can work. We will find each other no matter what. VO19: Fighting talk from GNU Minister Gayton Mackenzie. And while the effect on state schools remains to be seen, the Act’s supporters are impatient to see it implemented in full. UPSOUND EMIHLE MAJIKIJA (SECTION 27): It is really, really, really important for the transformation of basic education in this country. The National Assembly passed it, the NCOP passed it. There was already public consultation. Democracy worked and gave us the Bela Bill. What more can you possibly ask for?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A bill that sparked big debate with some saying it will cause the end of the government of national unity... but the emotions aside, does Government have the money to implement the controversial Bela
metadata.Unique Selling Point: What's all the hype about the Bela bill if government doesn't even have the money to implement it?
metadata.Summary: Its gonna cost resources... and lot of it... does government have the financial and administrative capacity to implement the controversial Bela Bill? Grade R is now compulsory. In the most ironic turn of events, government earmarks R16 billion necessary to establish infrastructure and appoint teachers to fill the gap. But at the same time, teacher retrenchments are underway. The Western Cape just announced the retrenchment of 2400 teacher due to budget cuts.
metadata.Further information: Two clauses of the Act were set aside for further discussion when president Cyril Ramaphosa signed the Basic Education Laws Amendment (Bela) Bill on Friday the 13th of September. One being admission and the other being the state's power to determine language proposed by a school SGB. The bill is only an amendment of an existing bill and much of it was already included in original bill of 1996. Now, there will be harsher punishment if the bill is not implemented. A parent for example, can now be jailed if a child is not sent to school. The onus was always on the parents, the consequences for failure to adhere, are just made much harsher and many organisations agree on this front. What most organisations, civil groups and activists don't agree with, is certain aspects of the bill that government does not have money to implement. The most concerning is that Grade R is now compulsory and it will cost government nearly 16 million Rand to to enforce this decision. It will mean classrooms and teachers- resources- in the midst of thousands of teachers that have to be laid off over the next few months. In Cape Town alone, over 2500 teachers have been retrenched. So how will funds be reprioritise in a province such as Gauteng, to make room for thousands of Grade R's? Further to this: If a parent fails to send their children to school, those parents must be identified and the local department of education must visit the parent, trying to establish reasons why the children are not in school. Then the legal system must kick in and parents must be prosecuted, what financial burden will this have on the state? Homeschooling: If a child is to be homeschooled, the Departmnet must register the home school. Then an assessor must be appointed to asses the homeschool. These are usually senior educators, are they going to be appointed? How many new appointments will this be within the department and how is the state to afford this? Lastly, if clause 4 and 5 are signed into law in 3 months, what will the financial burden be on schools and how will the state assist the schools financially? For example: if an Afrikaans medium school is forced to admit English or Zulu learners, capacity should be created within the school to accommodate these learners. Who will fund this and if its funded by the state, with what money? or will schools be forced to pay for these shortcomings themselves? will this be a further burden on parents to pay higher school fees?
metadata.Extra Budget Items: This shoot is scattered across days. We speak to the minister of basic education on 27 September. Then we speak to the MEC of education in Gauteng on 30 September and regarding language and admissions, we are able to speak to Afriforum-pivotal in the postponement of the signing of 4 and 5, on 26 September.
